summary: Collects advice for safely handling malformed email messages, recommending some tolerance rather than outright rejection. It is implementation guidance.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes letters are written badly. This says how to read them kindly anyway.

questions: how mta should treat bad messages
subtitle: Practical guidance for handling email messages that don't follow the rules.

tldr.problem: Email software often produces messages that violate format specifications, but strictly rejecting all malformed mail would break communication with legitimate senders.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7103 provides implementation guidance on how to handle common message malformations safely: fixing some, tolerating others, and detecting potential attacks.
tldr.outcome: Email systems can balance robustness with security by following structured advice on when to repair, reject, or work around specific malformation types.

today: RFC 7103 provides implementation guidance, not standards requirements. It remains a reference for how email systems can tolerate real-world malformations safely. The guidance applies to Mail Submission Agents, Mail Transfer Agents, and Mail User Agents handling non-standard messages.

sections.title: The Problem of Non-Standard Messages
sections.content:
Email specifications have been precise since the 1970s, but in practice, authoring and handling software often shows only mild compliance. Messages that deviate from standards reach users every day, yet strictly rejecting all non-standard messages would break legitimate communication with senders using flawed software.

This leads to a tension: Postel's Law advises being liberal in what you accept and conservative in what you send, but excessive tolerance can expose vulnerabilities to attack. The RFC addresses this by providing guidance on which malformations to tolerate, which to repair, and which to treat as warning signs.
sections.plainLanguage: Email is supposed to follow strict rules, but real software breaks them all the time. This shows how to read broken mail safely.

sections.title: The Role of Handling Stages
sections.content:
Messages pass through multiple handling stages: a Mail Submission Agent (MSA) accepts messages from users, Mail Transfer Agents (MTAs) relay them, and Mail User Agents (MUAs) present them to recipients. At each stage, a module can fix, alter, or reject malformed content.

A key principle is that all processing modules should see the same message content for analysis. If one module silently repairs a malformation, later modules lose the ability to detect malicious content that exploited that malformation. Additionally, when software differs in how it interprets a malformed message, an attacker can craft a single message that bypasses filters but misleads users.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail travels through many programs. They all need to see the same broken parts so they can spot problems.

sections.title: Header Anomalies and Fixes
sections.content:
The RFC catalogs dozens of malformations found in email headers. Examples include excessive or unbalanced angle brackets around addresses, unbalanced parentheses in comments, commas in the wrong places, and whitespace where it should not be.

For each, the RFC provides a recommended interpretation: removing extra angle brackets is safe, fixing unbalanced parentheses using comment syntax is reasonable, and treating isolated CR or LF as CRLF during parsing is practical. The core advice is to guide mitigation by the most likely semantic intent: if an address is obviously meant, extract it; if the intent is unclear or changing content is risky, leave it alone or reject.
sections.plainLanguage: Addresses sometimes have extra or missing brackets. These can usually be fixed by guessing what was meant.

sections.title: Dangerous Malformations: Repeated Fields
sections.content:
Some malformations carry security risks. When a message contains multiple From fields instead of one, different pieces of the mail system might believe different senders wrote it. A filter might check the first From and pass the message, but a user's mail reader might display the second, causing confusion or allowing impersonation.

The RFC recommends either rejecting such messages outright (the safest choice), removing excess instances, combining multiple values into one, or renaming violating fields so downstream agents ignore them. The choice depends on whether filtering, user display, or authentication properties are at risk.
sections.plainLanguage: If a message lists two senders instead of one, some mail programs might believe one and others believe the other.

sections.title: MIME, Character Sets, and Binary Data
sections.content:
MIME is the standard for attachments, non-ASCII text, and complex message structure. Common MIME malformations include a missing MIME-Version header when MIME constructs are present, incorrect or missing character set information, and 8-bit data where ASCII is required.

When charset information is wrong, the RFC advises checking if content is valid UTF-8 or detecting escape sequences used by specific Asian character sets. For 8-bit data in the header, options range from dropping the field to trying to decode it if a charset can be guessed. Special care is needed for null bytes and oversized lines, which can hide malicious content from analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages can contain pictures, different languages, and non-text attachments. When the labels are wrong, special handling is needed.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
The malformations described in this RFC exist partly because they exploit implementation differences. If the RFC recommends tolerating a deviation, it should not be a weakness but a calculated trade-off. However, some deviations are indicators of abuse: missing MIME-Version where MIME constructs appear, multiple conflicting senders, or oversized lines are often signs of malice.

The best practice is still for senders to follow standards strictly, for MSAs to enforce those standards, and for downstream handlers to apply these tolerances only when strictly necessary. Security filtering systems must be especially cautious, checking not just one interpretation of a message but potentially multiple, to detect attacks that exploit parsing differences.
sections.plainLanguage: Breaking the rules is sometimes done by mistake and sometimes on purpose to hide bad things.
